description: An account whose usage a version migration raises from 92 GB to 104 GB. The case fixes the number a durable receipt is refused against, and how that number comes back down.
notes: D81 promises that a migration alone never refuses an account. This vector is that promise turned into a number: without a persisted threshold, 'keeps accepting until its own writing crosses the line' does not say which line, and two implementations would disagree about when refusal starts.

account.grandfathered_threshold_units lives in the account row beside account.logical_usage_units. For every account never raised by a migration it equals the pool, so there is one rule and no special case.
Written at the migration switch inside the same single transaction as the new usage (contract 10.2 step 5), so no receipt can observe one without the other.

THE RATCHET IS THE ONE RULE THIS CONTRACT SUPPLIES RATHER THAN RECORDS. The CTO said usage-reducing operations bring an account back 'toward' 100 GB; 'toward' is directional but not exact. See contract 12.2 item L - it is flagged for correction at sign-off.

Consequence of the ratchet: while grandfathered, the account has NO headroom. It can converge, delete and reduce, but it cannot grow. That is correct - it is over its allowance, and grandfathering only stops it being refused for content it already had.

It cannot ratchet up. If it could, the account could delete to 98 and re-add, recovering headroom to 104 that it was never sold. Only a migration may raise it, and only by exactly the amount our own arithmetic moved.

Unchanged by this vector: a migration alone never refuses (D81), the notice list identifies affected accounts before the switch, local editing is never affected, and the usage-reducing staging lane is what carries the account from 104 back toward 100.
Figures are exact LU. Decimal GB throughout (D78): 1 GB = 1,000,000,000.

before_migration.note: an ordinary account: threshold equals the pool

migration.note: a hypothetical V2 that raises this account's usage; the value is known before the switch, which is what makes the notice list computable

derivation: at the switch (contract 10.2 step 5, one transaction):
the account is NOT refused by the switch (D81)
step 1 - a durable receipt leaving usage at 103,000,000,000:
step 2 - a durable receipt that would take usage to 105,000,000,000:
(it also exceeds the 104,000,000,000 the switch wrote, so the refusal holds under either reading)
usage and threshold both unchanged by a refusal
step 3 - the account deletes down to 98,000,000,000:
fully back to normal; ordinary headroom returns
alternative branch from the switch - the account deletes to 102,000,000,000 instead:

steps.operation: durable receipt leaving usage at 104 GB minus 1 GB
steps.why: 103 GB does not exceed the threshold of 104 GB; the ratchet then follows usage down

steps.operation: durable receipt that would take usage to 105 GB
steps.why: 105 GB exceeds the threshold; a refusal changes neither usage nor threshold

steps.operation: the account deletes down to 98 GB
steps.why: max(pool, min(103 GB, 98 GB)) = pool - fully back to normal, ordinary headroom returns

alternative_branch.operation: the account deletes down to 102 GB
alternative_branch.why: max(pool, min(104 GB, 102 GB)) = 102 GB - still partly grandfathered

invariants: grandfathered_threshold_units is never below the pool
grandfathered_threshold_units never increases except at a migration switch, and then only to max(pool, post_migration_usage)
a refusal changes neither usage nor threshold
local editing is never affected by any of this
an account that has never been raised by a migration has grandfathered_threshold_units == pool, so this is one rule with no special case
must_not: refuse the account on the strength of the migration itself (D81)
refuse against the pool rather than the threshold while the account is grandfathered
let the threshold rise when usage rises - deleting and re-adding must not restore headroom the account was never sold
let the threshold fall below the pool
